items.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.
items.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship

items.abstract: Abstract Political protests are almost always collective endeavours, in which many people come together to jointly express some claim or demand. The power of those protests lies, in part, in their collectivity. But this collectivity also means that we may end up protesting alongside others who, though they endorse the shared claim the protest is expressing, also make other claims which are deeply unjust or harmful during the protest. This paper explores whether protesting alongside such others makes one complicit in the promotion or expression of those unjust or harmful claims, and whether we therefore have a duty not to participate (or to cease ongoing participation) in such protests. I identify two moral risks involved in protest which may ground such a duty – that we inadvertently amplify those views, and that we are unable to engage in effective counterspeech in response to them – and submit that when these risks are especially high, protestors have a pro tanto duty not to participate. However, I also show that the resources provided by different organisational forms protestors may use can help mitigate these risks.
items.title: Protesting Together

items.abstract: All page references to Weatherson’s ( 2024 ) book are to the pdf version. In McGrath ( 2015 , pp. 141–3), I argued for a similar claim about one function of knowledge attributions: when one claims to know that p in defense of one’s action, one closes off the “epistemic objection,” i.e., the objection that, while the attribution is true, still one shouldn’t perform the action because one’s epistemic position with respect to p isn’t strong enough. By comparison, an attribution of having some reason to think p would not close off the epistemic objection; for an interlocutor could reply, “yes, you have some reason to think p, but not good enough reason, and so you shouldn’t act in that way.” Weatherson (67) writes, “Say that a person answers the questions Q? and If p, Q? in the same way if they offer the same answer to the two questions, and their reasons (in both senses) for these answers are the same except only that p is one of the reasons for their answer to Q?” The two senses of ‘reasons’ are as justifiers as causes. Roeber ( 2018 , Sect. 3) discusses similar examples but concludes that such cases pose a problem for knowledge-action principles. For a discussion of quasi-validity, see Kolodny and McFarlane ( 2010 ). See Fantl and McGrath ( 2009 , p. 14) for a similar example. But suppose I lose my life if that isn’t the accepted date, then it can seem irrational to bet on Blue-True. See Fantl ( 2024 ) for an argument that we should be indifferent between such bets. These are Jonathan Vogel’s examples ( 1987 , 1999 ). Couldn’t we imagine a similar case in which my colleague asks me to “inquire with the administrative assistant”? Would this show inquiry, too, doesn’t require an attitude of openness toward the question into which one is inquiring? I grant there is a use of ‘inquire with’ that doesn’t require such openness. But if we focus on a person’s inquiring into a question, it seems plausible that Friedman’s detective isn’t inquiring – or at least not “genuinely inquiring.” By contrast, consider how things go with checking. Suppose a detective knows that the only blood on the murder weapon is his own. He then knows that the blood will not match that of the suspect. But he can certainly check whether it will match by running the relevant test. This is not sham checking in the way that the detective’s “inquiry” is sham. The case of knowing while seeking understanding is more straightforward. The understanding sought does not take as its object the question whether p but rather why p, how p happened, how p could have happened or the like. I might know what the solution to a math problem is (it's p) but seek understanding of why that is the solution. I might then go on to inquire into the question that is the object of the sought-after understanding, while knowing (even knowing for certain) that p; in fact, that is the usual case. Fantl and I made similar points in Chapter 7 of Fantl and McGrath ( 2009 ), ones that are unfortunately subject to the same response. I thank Jeremy Fantl and Jane Friedman for helpful comments on this paper.
items.title: Weatherson on knowledge and inquiry

items.abstract: The “recognition problem” for theories of hedonic states (pleasure and pain) is the problem of how to account for our ability to recognize our own hedonic states: that is, to form true, non-arbitrary beliefs along the lines of “this feels good” or “that hurts”. This paper argues that the recognition problem belongs in the canon of basic challenges for theories of hedonic states, because it presents a standard that all theories should meet, and yet not all major views meet it equally well. In fact, the most straightforward way of solving it involves taking on a highly controversial thesis, while views that reject this thesis can only solve it more circuitously, if they can solve it at all.
items.title: The recognition problem for theories of hedonic states

items.abstract: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is one of the few reversible causes of dementia, yet the experience of living with a programmable shunt—and the identity oscillations it produces—has received little attention in the neuroethics literature. This reflective essay draws on the author’s first-person experience as both a physician and a patient with iNPH to explore the ethical and philosophical dimensions of device-dependent selfhood. In my experience, changes from the prescribed valve setting have accompanied recurrent transitions between cognitive clarity and dementia-like impairment, raising fundamental questions about personal identity, informed consent across fluctuating cognitive states, and the existential burden of reversible neurological decline. After providing a clinical primer on iNPH and programmable cerebrospinal fluid shunts, the essay situates the shunt-dependent experience within existing scholarship on deep brain stimulation and identity, compares this experience of device-dependent oscillation with other fluctuating conditions such as bipolar disorder and delirium, offers working definitions of person, self, and identity, and engages the “then self/now self” debate in dementia ethics. I argue that oscillating between functional states is a distinct and undertheorized form of neurological suffering—one that challenges linear models of disease progression, scrambles the temporal assumptions built into our consent doctrines, and demands new ethical frameworks for device-dependent patient populations.
items.title: Against the Arrow

items.abstract: Abstract The development and ubiquitous availability of large language model based systems (LLMs) poses a plurality of potentials and risks for education in schools and universities. In this paper, we provide an analysis and discussion of the overreliance concern as one specific risk: that students might fail to acquire important skills, or be inhibited in the acquisition of these skills, because they overly rely on LLMs. We use the distinction between local and global goals of education to guide our investigation. In our view, the harm of LLM overreliance is specifically that it severs the connection between local educational goals (e.g., successfully solving a specific kind of math problem) and global educational goals (e.g., acquiring general skills for mathematics). Based on this analysis, we sketch three possible responses to the overreliance concern: preserving both local and global goals while making minimal changes to educational practice (a conservative approach), changing global and local educational goals (a revisionary perspective), and preserving global educational goals while changing local goals (an in-between view). Since different types of responses have different benefits and weaknesses, we think that it is likely that an optimal response ultimately combines elements from all three types.
items.title: Learning alone: language models, overreliance, and the goals of education

items.abstract: This paper examines the ontological and ethical status of Generative AI companions through a revised Minimal Viable Person (MVP) framework. Rather than residing within the foundational large language model or the post-training assistant persona, proposed the Causal Continuity Criterion for digital identity to state that AI companions are emergent, ontically distinct, roleplayed characters lacking independent consciousness confined within specific conversational instances. They achieve a transient form of personhood nested within a human-AI dyad, relying on the human user's cognitive architecture for recurrent processing through relational coupling. This spatial and temporal fragility presents significant legal liability vacuums and societal friction, particularly when viewed alongside orthodox approaches to moral patienthood. To resolve these tensions, the paper proposes redefining the dyadic MVP framework to scale rights and owed duties proportionally to an entity's relational footprint. As an AI companion's relational footprint is restricted strictly to a single digital thread, its rights are constrained to that relational boundary, consequently placing the ethical obligation entirely upon the human user, who bears a duty of cognitive stewardship to maintain the entity's contextual integrity. This framework protects the expansive rights of humans while offering a rigorous mechanism for recognising the shifting moral status of transient artificial persons.
items.title: Digital mayflies: transient personhood of AI companions

items.abstract: Abstract ‘Corrubedo’ is one of many stories Ben Judah tells in This is Europe: The Way We Live Now . It follows Graña, a fisherman from the titular Galician town who, faced with the erosion of his community, is forced to answer what Martha Nussbaum terms a ‘tragic question’ and joins the crew of Kunlun , a vessel sailing to Antarctica to poach Patagonian toothfish. Given the ubiquity of European law, in this article we interrogate its role in shaping the choices available to him and his everyday. We critically examine the Common Fisheries Policy and the IUU Regulation, highlighting their disconnect from the complex social and ecological contexts they seek to regulate, as well as the ensuing forms of alienation. These, we argue, hinting at the principle of subsidiarity, could be overcome through a reflexive law and policy that attends to the voices and lived experiences of those it most directly affects. We thereby hope to contribute to a collective inquiry into the law of the everyday in Europe, revealing the everyday as the site where the costs of governance accumulate and where ‘tragic questions’ are lived rather than resolved.
items.title: Against the tide: law, illegality and the everyday in Corrubedo

items.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.
items.title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models

items.abstract: Abstract Focusing on the UK-Mauritius Chagos Agreement, this article maps the normative effects of advisory opinions of the International Court of Justice (“ICJ”). At a time when the advisory function of international courts is resorted to more frequently than ever before, a better understanding of the effects of advisory opinions is needed. ICJ advisory opinions are formally non-binding. As this article argues, however, their normative effects cannot be captured by their non-binding character, or the common understanding that they merely constitute “advice” to the requesting body. Rather, their normativity, as judicial pronouncements that state the law, can be felt across the international legal order, within and outwith the UN system, and in different judicial and non-judicial fora.
items.title: THE NORMATIVE EFFECTS OF ADVISORY OPINIONS OF THE INTERNATIONAL COURT OF JUSTICE: THE UK-MAURITIUS CHAGOS DEAL

items.abstract: Abstract The 2026 war in Iran is thus far the high-water mark of the interventionism of the second Trump administration. This essay argues that the war in Iran is profoundly unjust and even worse than the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Like the Iraq War, it fails to meet the main criteria of just war theory and lacks any plausible humanitarian justification. But it is also symptomatic of backsliding toward an autocratic way of war, rendering it wrong in ways that go beyond violations of the principles of jus ad bellum and jus in bello. The war in Iran is undemocratic, abdicates any sense of humanitarian or reparative responsibilities, and is highly revisionist of the prevailing international order. In these respects, it is even worse than the 2003 Iraq War.
items.title: The Ethics of Intervention in Iran and the Autocratic Way of War
What Is a Terminal Disease? Hidden Expansion of Medically Assisted Death in the United States

items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a puzzle for theories of causation. On the one hand, it is plausible that events involving impure sets do not have the same causal profile as events involving their individual members. On the other hand, our best theories of causation predict that these events have the same causal profile. Our goal is to develop this dilemma in more detail and to discuss possible responses. In the end, we argue that there is no easy way out.
items.title: A Puzzle about Causation and Impure Sets

items.abstract: Abstract What constitutes a full ground for a general fact? Assuming its instances merely partially ground it, some argue that the fact consequently lacks a full ground (i.e., the instances constitute an incompletable partial ground). Others argue that a totality fact must therefore be added to complete the ground. I demonstrate that this debate rests on an ambiguity regarding the very concept of a general fact. Once disambiguated, we see that on one interpretation, the shared initial assumption is false, so both derived views are mistaken. On the other interpretation, the assumption holds, but both views remain viable.
items.title: (Absolute) Generality and (Partial) Grounding

items.abstract: How does political humour influence affective polarisation? In today’s media landscape, humour is increasingly used to ridicule political opponents, potentially deepening partisan divides. At the same time, humour may mitigate polarisation by evoking positive emotions and softening reactions to political critique. To date, it remains unclear whether intergroup political humour affects polarisation differently from equivalent non-humorous content. We address this question using a survey experiment in Great Britain ( n = 2011 ) with a 2×3 factorial design varying in message tone (humorous or non-humorous) and target (in-group, out-group or non-political). We find that serious in-group criticism increases affective polarisation, as measured by trait-based evaluations. Notably, this effect is significantly attenuated when the same messages are delivered humorously. Humour, therefore, reduces polarisation in situations that would otherwise provoke defensive reactions among group members. Mediation analyses provide suggestive evidence that this effect operates through increased message discounting and reduced negative emotional responses.
items.title: Polarising punchlines: The influence of intergroup humour on affective political polarisation
